I have being to career fairs at my university. I am not sure how big is the career fair you are going to, but it should be the same process regardless. At this stage, it does not matter much how skilled of a worker you are.

The key is to do your research about the companies that are attending, make a compacted list of potential employers that you are interested in, and go to them first.

The day of the fair, dress sharp. Make sure your dress is clean and pressed. Have a small box of altoids in your pockets just in case. Don't forget to print enough copies of your resume, and that it is well formatted. The resume is what is going to represent you when you are not physically present around the recruiter.

Make your interaction brief and concise. From the moment you make eye contact with the recruiter, every second counts. Give a firm hand shake, and give a quick introduction of yourself (Your name, current occupation, what are you looking for, and why you consider yourself as a desirable new hire), hand the resume and make sure that you hit the nail on some of the bullets that would impress. During your interaction, try to be as relaxed as possible and try to make the interaction pleasurable, and don't be afraid to throw a joke or two if that fits your persona and a chance presents itself. You have to remember that most of the recruiters out there will have to talk to many potential hires and that takes a toll during the day (which is why it is good to have a list of desirable companies in handy, the earlier you approach them, the more likely for you to have a meaningful interaction). Be as enthusiastic as possible without overdoing it off course, just remember a period of time when you were enjoying an activity with your friends, and embody that feeling during the fair.

Post fair, it is good practice to get in touch with the recruiters you met during the fair. A short thank you email with a quick summary of why you are interested in the position and why you think they should hire you.

It is not out of the ordinary that you might get very few replies, or no replies at all for a follow up interview. Do not feel as if you failed. Sometimes (in reality I mean most of the time) HR can make some very arbitrary decisions on who to follow up with for the next hiring step. Keep on distributing your resume everywhere that seems to be a possible fit for your skill. Many people would attest, including my self, that when it comes to early stage careers, a big part of the hiring process is pure luck vs. the value you would bring to the company you might work for.

Stay focused and organized, and good luck.
